title: Cre-Dependent Expression of Multiple Transgenes in Isolated Neurons of the Adult Forebrain
abstract: BACKGROUND: Transgenic mice with mosaic, Golgi-staining-like expression of enhanced green fluorescent protein (EGFP) have been very useful in studying the dynamics of neuronal structure and function. In order to further investigate the molecular events regulating structural plasticity, it would be useful to express multiple proteins in the same sparse neurons, allowing co-expression of functional proteins or co-labeling of subcellular compartments with other fluorescent proteins. However, it has been difficult to obtain reproducible expression in the same subset of neurons for direct comparison of neurons expressing different functional proteins. PRINCIPAL FINDINGS: Here we describe a Cre-transgenic line that allows reproducible expression of transgenic proteins of choice in a small number of neurons of the adult cortex, hippocampus, striatum, olfactory bulb, subiculum, hypothalamus, superior colliculus and amygdala. We show that using these Cre-transgenic mice, multiple Cre-dependent transgenes can be expressed together in the same isolated neurons. We also describe a Cre-dependent transgenic line expressing a membrane associated EGFP (EGFP-F). Crossed with the Cre-transgenic line, EGFP-F expression starts in the adolescent forebrain, is present in dendrites, dendritic protrusions, axons and boutons and is strong enough for acute or chronic in vivo imaging. SIGNIFICANCE: This triple transgenic approach will aid the morphological and functional characterization of neurons in various Cre-dependent transgenic mice.

stewardship.abstract:
Background

Transgenic mice with mosaic, Golgi-staining-like expression of enhanced green fluorescent protein (EGFP) have been very useful in studying the dynamics of neuronal structure and function. In order to further investigate the molecular events regulating structural plasticity, it would be useful to express multiple proteins in the same sparse neurons, allowing co-expression of functional proteins or co-labeling of subcellular compartments with other fluorescent proteins. However, it has been difficult to obtain reproducible expression in the same subset of neurons for direct comparison of neurons expressing different functional proteins.

Principal findings

Here we describe a Cre-transgenic line that allows reproducible expression of transgenic proteins of choice in a small number of neurons of the adult cortex, hippocampus, striatum, olfactory bulb, subiculum, hypothalamus, superior colliculus and amygdala. We show that using these Cre-transgenic mice, multiple Cre-dependent transgenes can be expressed together in the same isolated neurons. We also describe a Cre-dependent transgenic line expressing a membrane associated EGFP (EGFP-F). Crossed with the Cre-transgenic line, EGFP-F expression starts in the adolescent forebrain, is present in dendrites, dendritic protrusions, axons and boutons and is strong enough for acute or chronic in vivo imaging.

Significance

This triple transgenic approach will aid the morphological and functional characterization of neurons in various Cre-dependent transgenic mice.

narrative_llm:
Short impact summary

This 2008 PLoS ONE article has shown steady scholarly uptake in neuroscience, with 16 citations in OpenAlex, 17 documented instances of downstream reuse, and at least one supporting citation statement in scite. Its influence is visible across a broad citation landscape that includes research articles, book chapters, preprints, a dissertation, and a review, suggesting that the method has been taken up as a practical tool rather than remaining a narrowly cited technical note.

Full narrative

Chakravarthy and colleagues addressed a technical bottleneck in studies of neuronal structure and plasticity: how to express multiple transgenes in the same sparse neurons of the adult forebrain without losing the mosaic, Golgi-like labeling that makes individual cells easy to study. The article’s central value lies in method development, and its downstream record reflects that role. Rather than drawing only on one niche, later works citing it span core neuroscience, tracing methods, optogenetics, chromatin biology, and neurodevelopmental research.

The citation pattern is modest in absolute terms but durable over time, with citations appearing from the publication year onward and continuing into recent years. That sustained use is consistent with a methods paper that remains relevant whenever investigators need Cre-dependent sparse labeling or multi-transgene expression in specific neuronal populations. The citing venues include journals and preprints such as bioRxiv, Cerebral Cortex, Nature Genetics, Reviews in the Neurosciences, European Journal of Neuroscience, and Nature Reviews Neuroscience, underscoring uptake in visible neuroscience and adjacent fields.

Reuse signals reinforce that interpretation. The article is documented as reused in 17 downstream works, including research articles and book chapters, and it is also indexed in Europe PMC as an article mention. The topics of citing works point toward practical experimental use: neuronal subtype manipulation, dendritic spine visualization, and studies of neural circuits and gene regulation. This is the kind of evidence one expects for a tool paper that contributes infrastructure to later experiments, even when the total citation count remains moderate.

The broader record is comparatively quiet outside scholarly channels. There are no event-data mentions recorded here, and the evidence base does not show a large public-discussion footprint. The article is open access and widely archived across repositories, which likely supported discoverability, but the clearest story in the data is its method-oriented scholarly afterlife: a technically focused paper that continued to inform experimental neuroscience over many years.
